title: This 911 Call Would Forever Haunt Officers
description:
Submit a tip! Tips@Midwest-Safety.com

Please consider JOINING for $1 a month. It *really* helps us do original reporting like this. 

CONTACT US:
Complaints? Video submissions? Sponsorships? Collabs? Business inquires? 
Email our board at mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com. 

BE NICE:
The individuals presented in these videos may be suffering from the effects of alcohol, drug abuse, a mental health disorder or simply having a bad day. The videos should NOT be presumed to be representative of their general behavior. Everyone deserves to be treated with respect. 

RIGHT TO BE FORGOTTEN:
Midwest Safety practices the "Right to be Forgotten." If you were the suspect in a lower-level offense, you may email our board to request removal. 
Email: mn.safety.alerts@gmail.com

Both the suspect, 57-year-old Anthony George, and the four-year-old victim, Terrell Miller, were pronounced dead at the scene. When officers entered, Kayana Miller, Terrell's mother, was covered in blood. Having been stabbed multiple times, Anthony George was holding a knife when Officer Gok ordered him to drop it. George then grabbed Terrell holding a knife to the child's throat. Officer Gock fired a single round, striking both George and Terrell instantly. killing them both. George had an extensive criminal history and had previously pleaded guilty to murder in 1995. His most recent charge was for domestic battery in November 2023. Journal investigations concluded that the shooting was justified and did not violate department policy. One investigator stated, now as to Terrell Miller, that was found to be accidental. I don't think in any way, shape, or form anyone felt that the officer's intent was to go in there and hurt young Miller. While no action will be taken against the officers involved, Kayana Miller, Terrell's mother, has filed a lawsuit against the officer who fired the shot. The case will be decided in federal court. Now, this is something no cop wants to have to live with. I know firsthand that the cause that sound vague are the ones that most likely stay with you forever. There are moments in policing when the sound of a single word or a sentence can slice through your chest like glass. And I've been there before hearing screams behind locked doors knowing that something terrible was unfolding just feet away but hidden from sight. And it's the most powerless feeling in the job because you don't know if you're about to save a life or walk into a nightmare that scars you forever. We see a man who puts a knife to a child and that probably doesn't feel real even when you're standing right there. There was no pause to process, no luxury of debate. just a split second to end the threat. People watching from the outside think that split-second decisions are measured in bravery, but they're not. They're measured in impossibility because do you risk one life to save another? Do you hold your fire and risk watching someone die right in front of you? Or do you fire and carry the weight of everything that follows? And I've left scenes before with a real horror unfolded after I was gone. Moments that remind me how thin the threat of survival really is in this line of work. But when I see cases like this, I think about the opposite, because what happens when you stay, when you step in and you're the one forced to make the choice that changes lives forever? Now, you guys will probably replay this scene a hundred times on your TV or phone. But the officers lived it once with no pause button, no rewind, and no chance to edit the outcome. And that's the reality, because what takes the world hours to dissect, a cop has less than a heartbeat to decide. There's no winners and tragedies like this because a child's life was lost, and an officer will carry that weight in his chest until his last breath.
